clue.text: His written grammar was exemplary: spoken, less tasteful

indicators.note: spoken tells the solver to say a word out loud and write down the different spelling it matches

blocks.note: something less tasteful is more foul, the comparative of foul

explanation.surface: A grammarian whose prose was a model, yet whose speech was rather coarse.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Fowler wrote Modern English Usage, the classic British guide to grammar and style.
explanation.definitionFit: Fowler's usage manual became the standard reference, making the author a byword for correct English writing.

clue.text: Two revolutionaries gamely throwing projectiles from here

blocks.note: first revolutionary: a ring, a shape that goes round and round
second revolutionary: Guevara, the Marxist guerrilla leader

explanation.surface: A pair of rebels lobbing missiles from a hiding place, as if playing a game.
explanation.walkthrough: One phrase supplies both pieces: a circle that revolves, then the famous Argentine revolutionary.
explanation.definitionFit: The oche is the line behind which a darts player stands, so it is where missiles are thrown in a game.

clue.text: Bridge players' call to judgement?

blocks.note: at the card table, the final card of the master suit left in a hand
the trumpet blast that summons the dead on Judgement Day

explanation.surface: Card players at the table making a bid that settles who wins.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is a biblical one (1 Corinthians 15:52) but reads naturally as a term from trick-taking card games.
explanation.definitionFit: Scripture says a final trumpet will sound to raise the dead for divine judgement, and that same phrase suits a card player's final top-suit card.

clue.text: Thatcher as Red Queen absorbing energy

indicators.note: a word absorbing something takes it inside itself, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
E is the physics symbol for energy
ER, Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: Margaret Thatcher cast as the Red Queen of Alice, soaking up vigour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thatcher' looks like the prime minister, but it is a roofer working with reeds.
explanation.definitionFit: A reeder is a craftsman who roofs houses with reeds or straw, which is exactly a thatcher's trade.

clue.text: The Camptown plum puller whose stock has points taken off?

definitions.text: whose stock has points taken off?

blocks.note: the minstrel song Camptown Races sings 'de' for 'the', as in 'de doo-dah day'
Little Jack Horner, in the nursery rhyme, put in his thumb and pulled out a plum

explanation.surface: A puzzling character from the Camptown song who yanks out plums.
explanation.walkthrough: Stock here is livestock, and points are the horns removed from cattle.
explanation.definitionFit: Farmers remove horns from cattle so they cannot injure each other, and the person or tool doing it is a dehorner.

clue.text: One might show contrition for auntie's bloomers, perhaps, and glee with ITC error

definitions.text: One might show contrition for auntie's bloomers

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters that follow might be arranged some other way

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; the Independent Television Commission, which regulated commercial TV
taken as written

explanation.surface: A broadcasting chief apologising for blunders, while a rival regulator gloats over the mistakes.
explanation.walkthrough: Auntie is the British nickname for the BBC. 'Perhaps' looks like it qualifies the bloomers, and 'error' like an anagram signal, but 'error' is part of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The head of the BBC holds the title director-general, and is the one expected to apologise publicly for its gaffes.

clue.text: So with Mom''s apple pie, weed out what makes me mad

indicators.note: out here means outside, so the gardening word wraps around the rest

blocks.note: to weed with a garden tool is to hoe
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook irritated by weeds and by the cliché of mother's apple pie.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the phrase 'as American as Mom's apple pie': this pie is the classic kitchen-baked kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Mother's apple pie is the archetype of food baked in the family kitchen rather than bought from a shop.

clue.text: He's OK

blocks.note: first meaning: a man's first name, so a he
second meaning: the radio operator's word for message received and understood

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a verdict on some man; really it pairs a male name with radio-speak for agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a common boy's name, and in radio procedure it signals acknowledgement, much like saying all right.

clue.text: Morecambe and Wise, we hear, sag from this blooming characterisation

definitions.note: a noun phrase for an adjective: the answer is the characterisation itself

indicators.note: we hear means the word is matched only by its spoken sound, not spelling
taking a word from another means removing those letters

blocks.note: the comedian Eric Morecambe
wise in a longer synonym, the partner's surname read as an adjective, spelt as the plant ending
taken as written, the letters to be removed

explanation.surface: The comedy double act Morecambe and Wise sagging and wilting, like flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: Eric plus sagacious without SAG gives ERIC-ACIOUS, which sounds like the botanical word. Morecambe and Wise were a much-loved British TV comedy duo.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes plants of the heather family, so it is a botanical characterisation of certain flowering shrubs.

clue.text: Nimrod dished "avec vin blanc et champignons"

blocks.note: first meaning: a huntsman, Nimrod being the mighty hunter of Genesis
second meaning: served in a sauce of white wine and mushrooms

explanation.surface: A hunter served up in a French sauce of white wine and mushrooms.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for a hunter also names the hunter-style sauce with mushrooms and white wine, so dishes are cooked in that style.

clue.text: One for sorrow among the chattering classes

blocks.note: first meaning: the counting rhyme says one bird seen means sorrow
second meaning: a noisy, chattering kind of bird

explanation.surface: A lone figure of grief among the talkative liberal intelligentsia.
explanation.walkthrough: The chattering classes are opinionated intellectuals in the surface; here they are the noisy birds.
explanation.definitionFit: The bird's nursery rhyme begins with one bringing sorrow, and it is notorious for its harsh chattering call.

clue.text: Cracked Matterhorn with Roman Catholic artillery

indicators.note: something cracked is broken apart, so these letters are smashed and rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written
RC is the standard abbreviation for Roman Catholic

explanation.surface: An Alpine peak shattered by guns belonging to a Catholic force.
explanation.definitionFit: A trench mortar is a short gun firing shells high over enemy lines, a piece of field weaponry.

clue.text: Faced paralysis, so possibly left bypass hell without beginning

indicators.note: possibly says the letters could form something else when rearranged
without its beginning means the first letter is dropped

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for left
taken as written
the word loses its opening letter

explanation.surface: Someone stricken by paralysis wondering if they could leave hell by a detour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Faced' is a coined adjective, of the face, so the definition means facial paralysis.
explanation.definitionFit: This condition is a sudden weakness of the facial nerve, causing one side of the face to droop.

clue.text: Rugby training switched in the country

indicators.note: switched means the two short pieces trade places, the second written first

blocks.note: PE, physical education, school training
RU is Rugby Union

explanation.surface: Rugby practice moved out to the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The country' looks like rural land; it is a nation in South America.
explanation.definitionFit: Peru is a South American nation, so it is a country in the sense of a sovereign state.

clue.text: No chicken with turnip?

blocks.note: first meaning: no spring chicken, someone getting on in years
second meaning: a turnip is slang for a fat old-fashioned pocket watch

explanation.surface: A dish of no chicken, served with turnip instead.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: an antique watch is literally an old timepiece.
explanation.definitionFit: A veteran is someone no longer young, and a bulky antique pocket watch is jokingly an old timepiece too.

clue.text: Cromwell's cavalry fell, as it were

blocks.note: first meaning: the nickname of Oliver Cromwell's troopers in the English Civil War
second meaning: to fell is to flatten, as pressing the flanks flat would

explanation.surface: Cromwell's horsemen fell in battle, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a verb phrase it is 'iron sides', pressing flat, which is a playful way to fell someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Cromwell's disciplined mounted troops earned this nickname, and literally pressing flanks flat is knocking down, loosely.

clue.text: Some queue outside here to displace Archimedes?

definitions.text: Some queue outside here to displace Archimedes?

blocks.note: surface: a place people line up for, waiting their turn
setter's reading: the room with the tub in which Archimedes famously displaced water

explanation.surface: People waiting in line to push a famous Greek mathematician out of somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Archimedes discovered displacement while getting into his tub; here people queue to take his place in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Households queue for the room with the tub each morning, and getting into a tub displaces its occupant's own volume of water.

clue.text: Carelessly applying make-up and hairstyle

blocks.note: slap is theatrical slang for greasepaint, make-up
a bang is a straight-cut fringe

explanation.surface: Someone slapdash in putting on cosmetics and doing their hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Done in a headlong, reckless way, without care, which is the adverbial sense of slap-bang.

clue.text: Lister's work applying oxygen to suppuration

blocks.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
suppuration is the forming of pus

explanation.surface: Joseph Lister's surgical research, treating festering wounds with oxygen.
explanation.walkthrough: Joseph Lister pioneered antiseptic surgery, which fits the medical surface; 'applying' and 'to' just set oxygen before the matter.
explanation.definitionFit: Opus is the Latin for a work, used of a composer's numbered compositions.

clue.text: Donkey, for one, bearing trap in Tyneside

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: east, a compass bearing
Tyneside is in the North East of England
a gin is a snare or trap

explanation.surface: A donkey in Newcastle carrying a cart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Donkey' looks like the animal, but a donkey engine is a small auxiliary engine on a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A donkey engine is a small steam engine used for hoisting on ships, so it is one example of the machine.

clue.text: Dressing so flashily no use in new penthouse suite development

indicators.note: with no use, the three letters spelling that word are taken away
development turns the material into something new and different

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for new
taken as written
the word with the letters of 'use' removed

explanation.surface: A developer's flashy new penthouse suite turns out to be useless.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone dressed elaborately and showily, in their very finest clothes.

clue.text: Swimmer more steamed up in Stepney

indicators.note: Stepney is in London's Cockney East End, where speakers drop the H

blocks.note: steamed up means hot, and more of it is the comparative

explanation.surface: A swimmer getting more and more worked up in an East London district.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys drop the opening H, so the comparative is said 'otter there.
explanation.definitionFit: The otter is a river mammal that spends much of its life in water, an expert swimmer.

clue.text: Chinese family worth £100,000?

blocks.note: a ton is slang for a hundred pounds
G, a grand, is a thousand; a hundred times a thousand makes the sum

explanation.surface: A wealthy Chinese clan valued at a hundred thousand pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: Pieces multiply rather than add: a ton (£100) of grand (£1,000) makes £100,000.
explanation.definitionFit: A tong is a Chinese secret society or fraternal association, a brotherhood bound like kin.

clue.text: Meeting one's fate in Switzerland? O, fate!

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: CH is the international code for Switzerland
one's lot is one's destiny
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone meeting their doom in the Alps, crying out against destiny.
explanation.walkthrough: The final 'fate' is the definition with a capital lost at the start: Clotho is one of the three Fates of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Clotho was one of the three Moirai, the Greek goddesses who spun, measured and cut the thread of life.

clue.text: Herald of St Swithun's reign might ordain priest for sacrifice

indicators.note: offered up for sacrifice, the words are destroyed and remade in a new form

blocks.note: taken as written
PR is an abbreviation for priest

explanation.surface: A saint's coming reign heralded by ordaining a priest to be sacrificed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reign' puns on rain: folklore says that if it rains on St Swithun's Day (15 July) it will rain for forty days.
explanation.definitionFit: The first drop of water falling on St Swithun's Day announces the forty wet days the old saying predicts.

clue.text: Alter ego literally left without memory ?- it's the drink!

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so the pieces surround something

blocks.note: Mr Hyde, Dr Jekyll's alter ego in Stevenson's story, so a literary one
L is the abbreviation for left
ROM, read-only memory in a computer

explanation.surface: Someone's other self, left with no memory, blaming it on alcohol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Literally' means from literature, pointing to Jekyll's sinister other self.
explanation.definitionFit: Hydromel is an old name for a fermented honey-and-water beverage, mead.

clue.text: Officer contributing to Dolly Varden''s ignominy

indicators.note: the letters contributing to the phrase lie inside it, spanning two words

blocks.note: the run spans the end of the surname and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: A naval officer playing a part in a Dickens heroine's disgrace.
explanation.walkthrough: Dolly Varden is a character in Dickens's Barnaby Rudge.
explanation.definitionFit: An ensign is a junior commissioned officer, the lowest such rank in the US Navy and formerly the British infantry.
